why: Weak property rights signal deteriorating rule of law and elite predation, conditions that historically precede political crises, mass protest, and institutional collapse. As a V-Dem expert-survey index it captures the subjective reality that citizens and investors face, not just formal legal text.
coverage_note: Near-universal V-Dem coverage from 1900; post-WWII country expansion means most countries from 1945+; very sparse for microstates pre-1970.

trends.reason: Property rights erosion is a direct structural correlate of corruption regimes; strong theoretical and empirical link.
Property rights contraction reliably precedes and accompanies power consolidation; captures the legal dismantling step.
Declining property rights accompany the crackdown environment but are partially redundant with other civil-liberties V-Dem signals.
Land seizures, expropriation, and property insecurity motivate protest mobilization especially in middle-income countries.
Tangential via investment-chilling effect; economic channels captured more directly by growth/credit variables.

why: Terms-of-trade shifts determine the real purchasing power of a country's exports and are a leading driver of fiscal stress, currency pressure, and social unrest in commodity-dependent states — exactly the macro shock profile preceding economic crises and political turbulence.
coverage_note: WB WDI coverage concentrated on goods-exporting economies; service-dominant and small-island states often missing; pre-1980 sparse.

trends.reason: ToT deterioration directly compresses foreign-exchange earnings, is a textbook currency-crisis precursor; strong causal channel.
Commodity ToT collapses are among the most reliable recession triggers for resource-exporting countries.
Revenue shortfalls from ToT decline force austerity or deficit spending; policy response often a data-visible event.
ToT-driven import price spikes translate to food/fuel cost-of-living pressure that fuels street mobilization.
Indirect pathway via economic grievance; signal is partially diluted by many intervening variables.

why: The current account balance in absolute USD captures the scale of a country's external financing gap or surplus, making it a direct precursor to balance-of-payments crises, IMF programme entry, currency devaluations, and associated political shocks that are disproportionately large in absolute-dollar terms for bigger economies.
coverage_note: Near-universal WB WDI coverage from ~1980; small island states and post-Soviet countries join from 1990/1992; absolute USD series can be noisy for dollarised economies.

trends.reason: Sustained large current-account deficits are the canonical BoP vulnerability signal that precedes currency crises.
Current account reversals often accompany sudden-stop financial crises and banking sector stress.
Abrupt CAB deterioration is a coincident-to-leading recession signal, especially for import-heavy economies.
Sanctions regimes visibly compress export receipts and shift the CAB; the absolute-USD series captures scale of impact.
CAB feeds fiscal narrative but the link is indirect; government revenue channels more directly covered by other fiscal indicators.

why: The Multidimensional Poverty Index captures the acute deprivation that conventional income measures miss — poor health, low education, and inadequate living standards simultaneously — providing a structural fragility baseline that predicts the susceptibility of a population to mobilization under stress events.
coverage_note: Coverage limited to low- and lower-middle-income countries where household surveys exist; high-income OECD countries absent; irregular survey rounds mean time series has gaps (often 3-5 year intervals, not annual).

trends.reason: MPI is the definitional measure of multidimensional poverty; directly models the state this Trend event describes.
High MPI countries are overwhelmingly the sites of humanitarian crises; strong baseline fragility signal.
Accumulated deprivation lowers the threshold for grievance-driven protest mobilization under trigger shocks.
MPI's food/health components directly overlap with famine vulnerability; high-MPI populations have lowest coping capacity.
Structural deprivation feeds insurgent recruitment but MPI is slow-moving vs. the dynamic conflict variables.

why: Normalizing conflict IDP stock by population converts a size-confounded count into a per-capita displacement intensity that is cross-nationally comparable and more directly reflects the state capacity collapse, territorial control loss, and sustained violence that define protracted political crises.
coverage_note: IDMC conflict stock series starts 2009 and covers ~150 conflict-affected countries; countries with zero displacement are inherently absent, creating a structural zero-inflation issue for ML preprocessing.

trends.reason: Per-capita IDP stock is the most direct observable of sustained internal conflict; strong signal for onset and persistence.
Conflict displacement at population scale is a definitional component of humanitarian crises; very strong empirical link.
Population-scale displacement often accompanies or follows systematic repression campaigns; correlated but non-identical.
IDP stocks are upstream of cross-border refugee flows; normalised version improves comparability for this Trend.
High IDP stocks trigger peace interventions but causality is reverse; marginal as a predictor of the event itself.

why: UNHCR's IDP stock normalized by population provides a governance-sourced view of internal displacement intensity that complements IDMC's figure — when both series agree, confidence in the displacement signal increases; divergence flags data quality issues for quality-control in the ML pipeline.
coverage_note: UNHCR IDP stock is limited to countries where UNHCR has operational presence and a mandate; coverage far narrower than IDMC (~80 countries vs 150+); significantly correlated with IDMC_CONF_STOCK_POP so feature collinearity is a concern.

trends.reason: Captures displacement at the high end of the severity spectrum where UNHCR has declared its mandate; valid conflict intensity signal.
UNHCR's mandate-based IDP coverage is specifically for the most severe humanitarian crisis contexts.
IDP pressure precedes and correlates with cross-border refugee movements; normalised ratio improves cross-country comparability.
UNHCR IDP presence implies repression in many cases but the series is too narrow geographically to be a primary signal.
UNHCR presence correlates with peace operations but adds little marginal signal beyond conflict and humanitarian variables.

why: The Atkinson-based income inequality measure used in the IHDI captures distributional skew that Gini misses at the extremes, and is a known predictor of grievance-driven unrest: societies where income concentration accelerates are more susceptible to populist mobilization, elite-mass conflict, and social instability.
coverage_note: UNDP HDR coverage ~150 countries but survey-dependent — high-income and conflict countries have gaps; annual interpolation used between survey rounds, reducing temporal precision; distinct from GINI so not redundant with WB series.

trends.reason: Direct measure of income inequality that defines this Trend category; strongest theoretical fit.
Empirical literature consistently links rising inequality to protest mobilization; Atkinson measure captures top-tail concentration especially relevant.
Income inequality is a direct driver of wage-dispute strikes and labour mobilisation; captures the distributional grievance.
High pre-existing inequality can amplify recession severity but the reverse channel is stronger; tangential signal.
Corruption and inequality co-evolve but INEQ_INC is an outcome variable not a direct corruption signal.

why: Deaths from violent political protests sit below the armed-conflict threshold but above routine demonstrations, marking the inflection zone where state-civilian tension escalates — this sub-conflict violence level is a leading indicator of full conflict onset and political regime instability.
coverage_note: Derived from UCDP GED events classified as political protests with lethal outcomes; available wherever GED has coverage (~145 countries); zero-inflated — peaceful countries will record zero for most years.

trends.reason: Lethal protest events are the direct quantitative measure of violent mobilization defining this Trend; high specificity.
Protest fatalities frequently arise from state repression of demonstrators; strong bidirectional signal.
Sub-conflict lethal protest deaths are a primary component of political violence Trend; near-definitional link.
Protest-driven violence often precedes or accompanies democratization episodes; useful leading signal.
Escalating protest violence is a recognized early-stage conflict escalation signal; moderate predictive value.

why: Freedom of expression captures the information environment available to citizens and opposition actors: its contraction is a hallmark of autocratization and political repression episodes, while its expansion is a necessary precondition for democratic transitions — making it a versatile leading indicator across multiple political risk Trends.
coverage_note: V-Dem near-universal coverage from 1900; reliable from ~1945 onwards for most countries; microstates and island nations may have thinner expert coverage pre-1990.

trends.reason: Media suppression and speech restriction are definitional elements of repression regimes; direct causal link.
Declining free expression is a canonical early step in autocratization and power consolidation sequences.
Freedom of expression improvements are both a signal and a precondition of democratic opening; useful transition predictor.
Sudden crackdowns on expression can trigger protest mobilization; expanding expression also enables protest coordination.
Press freedom restrictions and speech suppression are core human rights violations; moderate conceptual overlap.

why: Social protection coverage determines how much of the population has a buffer when economic or climate shocks hit — countries with thin coverage are far more vulnerable to shock-triggered unrest, labour conflict, and humanitarian crises, making this a key structural resilience signal in the QGI pool.
coverage_note: ILOSTAT modelled estimates cover ~180 countries but many data-poor countries rely on imputed ILO models rather than survey data; early years (pre-2005) have wider confidence intervals; sex-disaggregated breakdowns available for a subset.

trends.reason: Low social protection coverage is the structural foundation of poverty crises; captures state welfare capacity directly.
Absence of social protection drives workers to strike action as the only available income security mechanism.
Austerity-driven cuts to social protection are a direct protest trigger; coverage level is the baseline exposure.
Populations with zero social protection coverage are the most exposed when humanitarian shocks materialise.
Coverage changes capture reform outcomes but the Trend is better predicted by institutional change signals than coverage level per se.
